clips.title: Simplifying distributed systems development with Temporal's durable execution
clips.why: Tom Wheeler from Temporal takes a six-line function and adds what it needs to survive real failures, which is the code you would write for Nova's three-day run without Temporal.
look: Count what gets added to the short first version: retries, saved state, timers. Each one is a piece of the do-it-yourself version from this lesson.
The last minute asks what happens when the application crashes in the middle of the process. That is the deploy on Monday afternoon.
clips.after: Our ticketToPr stays close to the short version, because Temporal holds the state, the retries and the timers for us.

clips.title: What Is a Workflow in Temporal? A Clear Explanation
clips.why: A short, clear example of a run with two steps that must each happen exactly once, and how the event history makes sure they do.
look: The money example: a crash after the first step must not repeat the first step. writePlan in the lab is the same.
How Temporal recreates the state from the event history, so a finished step is not done again.
clips.after: Swap the withdrawal for writePlan and the deposit for openPr, and this is nova:RH-1234 surviving a deploy.

clips.title: Temporal in 7 Minutes - the TL;DR Intro
clips.why: The programming model in under two minutes: workflows, activities and workers, and who runs what.
look: Workflows are code that decides; activities are the calls that can fail.
Workers are your processes. The Temporal Service only stores and hands out work.
clips.after: In our platform the orchestrator is the set of workers, and the Jira poll and the Slack app are the clients.

clips.title: Simplifying distributed systems development with Temporal's durable execution
clips.why: The same talk explains what happens behind the scenes after a crash: the history is replayed and the finished steps are not done again.
look: Listen for the event history: every finished step is written down by the service, not by your process.
Watch how a new process reaches the same point by replaying, without calling the finished steps again.
clips.after: This is exactly what you do in the lab: kill the worker during the sleep, start it again, and see writePlan answered from the history.

practice.q: Which of these must be an activity, and not code inside the workflow?

options.why: It talks to the outside world and could answer differently later, so it runs once in an activity and its result is recorded.

options.text: Choosing to plan again when the requester presses Change
options.why: That is a decision based on what already happened. Decisions are the workflow's job.

options.text: Waiting three days for the requester to approve
options.why: Waiting is a durable timer inside the workflow. The service keeps it; no activity is needed.

practice.q: Finish the line that gives the workflow its stand-ins for the activities.
practice.hint: It comes from @temporalio/workflow, and its name says that it gives back proxies for activities.
practice.why: proxyActivities returns functions that ask Temporal to run the real activity on a worker and wait for the recorded result. The workflow never runs activity code itself.

practice.q: Put the events of nova:RH-1234's history in the order the service records them.
items: WorkflowExecutionStarted: the Jira poll started the run
TimerStarted: the workflow began its sleep
TimerFired: the sleep is over, even though no worker was running
WorkflowExecutionCompleted: the run returned its result
practice.why: The history is the run's story, written by the service as it happens. A replay walks through it in the same order and reaches the same point.

practice.q: The worker is stopped while nova:RH-1234 sleeps for three days. Where is the timer?

options.text: In the worker's memory, as a setTimeout
options.why: Then it would die with the worker. A durable timer is stored by the service.

options.text: In the Temporal Service, which fires it even when no worker is running
options.why: The service records TimerStarted and later TimerFired. The next worker that comes back sees the fired timer and continues.

options.text: In the client that started the run
options.why: The client left right after the start. It holds nothing about the run.

practice.q: Workflow code calls Date.now() and a new worker replays the run two days later. What does Date.now() return during the replay?

options.text: The time of the replay, two days later
options.why: That would make the replay decide differently from the first run. The SDK prevents this inside workflows.

options.text: The same time it returned the first time, because the SDK uses the time recorded in the history
options.why: In the workflow sandbox, Date.now() gives the time recorded for the current step, so a replay sees the same value.

options.text: It throws, because time is not allowed in workflows
options.why: It works; the SDK replaces it with a deterministic version. fetch and Node modules are the things that are really missing.
